Speaker: Marina Ganeva
Title: AI-assisted data pipelines for neutron experiments
Abstract: The lack of neutron beam time as well as the complexity of neutron scattering data processing make the development of AI assisted approaches to optimize the use of beam time at different stages of the scientific workflow inevitable. At MLZ, we build AI assisted data pipelines for data acquisition and analysis that enable fast, robust and reliable data processing on-the-fly during the experiment as well as offline. This allows experiment steering during beam time and accelerates offline data analysis. In this talk I will give an overview of our activities on establishing AI-assisted data pipelines for different neutron scattering techniques, such as TAS, small-angle and surface scattering.

Speaker: Tim Snow
Title: Nuts and Bolts: Infrastructure Platforms for Different Latency Regimes
Abstract: Each application of an AI or ML algorithm may seem unique, however, to sustain these in the long run there has to be some commonality as to how they are deployed and maintained. This talk investigates Diamond's (and to a lesser extent other facilities) approaches to this challenge, illustrating how solutions have been developed and tool chained with respect to latency. From very low latency, i.e. nano- to micro-seconds, to accepted latency, i.e. a known number of milliseconds, through to latency is acceptable, i.e. seconds onwards. I hope for a robust discussion after the main presentation!

Speaker: Taner Yildirim
Title: Evaluating the Performance of Universal Machine Learning Potentials in Neutron Scattering Spectra Predictions
Abstract: Machine learning-based atomic potentials have become essential for predicting the structure and dynamics of various materials. These potentials, which promise "ab initio accuracy with the efficiency of classical force fields," raise concerns about their true generalizability across a wide range of materials. Generalizability is crucial for extrapolating learned information to new systems, as it reduces the need for extensive training data for each material, thereby improving efficiency and applicability. To evaluate these claims, we rigorously tested several machine learning-based atomic potentials, calculating structural and lattice dynamic properties for a dozen diverse systems and comparing the results with our own neutron scattering data. In this talk, we will present our findings and offer suggestions for improvement, as none of the tested ML-based potentials provided satisfactory results.

Speaker: Viktor Reshniak
Title: Unsupervised Machine Learning for Automated Bragg Peak Identification and Integration in Time-of-Flight Neutron Scattering
Abstract: Accurate identification and integration of Bragg peaks are essential for extracting crystallographic information from time-of-flight (TOF) neutron scattering experiments. We present an unsupervised machine learning method that operates directly on raw data without requiring pre-training on external datasets. By leveraging a multi-scale, scale-space representation, our approach captures correlations and redundancies across different scales and reciprocal space (Q-space), enabling robust detection of both strong and weak Bragg peaks. The method is minimally dependent on prior information and human intervention, making it highly adaptable to diverse experimental conditions. We demonstrate its effectiveness on challenging datasets containing background artifacts and satellite peaks, highlighting the potential for improved reliability and efficiency in neutron scattering data analysis.

Speaker: Kamal Choudhary
Affiliation: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Title: DiffractGPT: Atomic Structure Determination from X-ray Diffraction Patterns Using a Generative Pretrained Transformer
Abstract: Crystal structure determination from powder diffraction patterns is a complex challenge in materials science, often requiring extensive expertise and computational resources. This study introduces DiffractGPT, a generative pretrained transformer model designed to predict atomic structures directly from X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns. By capturing the intricate relationships between diffraction patterns and crystal structures, DiffractGPT enables fast and accurate inverse design. Trained on thousands of atomic structures and their simulated XRD patterns from the JARVIS-DFT data set, we evaluate the model across three scenarios: (1) without chemical information, (2) with a list of elements, and (3) with an explicit chemical formula. The results demonstrate that incorporating chemical information significantly enhances prediction accuracy. Additionally, the training process is straightforward and fast, bridging gaps between computational, data science, and experimental communities. This work represents a significant advancement in automating crystal structure determination, offering a robust tool for data-driven materials discovery and design. DiffractGPT is available at: https://github.com/usnistgov/atomgpt

Speaker: Julian Heger
Title: Bringing Clarity to Complexity: Machine Learning-Supported Insight into Biohybrid Film Formation in Real Time with GISAXS
Abstract: Grazing-incidence X-ray small-angle scattering (GISAXS) is a powerful tool to study the structure of nano- and mesoscale materials, such as thin films used in energy devices. Thanks to the high brilliance of synchrotron sources, GISAXS can capture the formation of these films in real time and test their stability during operation or varying environmental conditions. For example, GISAXS examines flexible substrates to understand how mechanical deformation affects optoelectronic coatings [1], and it monitors the low-temperature formation of titania films during sustainable, water-based spray deposition [2, 3]. However, GISAXS has a major challenge: it loses phase information during measurement, which complicates the analysis needed to determine the sample's exact structure. In addition, typically large amount of data is acquired on short time scales. This problem makes the data analysis process both time-consuming and demanding, often requiring significant expertise. To overcome this, we have developed a machine learning approach that uses neural networks trained on synthetic data to analyze 2D GISAXS patterns in real time. Our goal is to provide an on-the-fly analysis during measurements at the synchrotron, making this powerful technique more accessible to a broader scientific community, including those without specialized experience in data interpretation. The talk presents our progress in using machine learning to support the analysis of time-resolved GISAXS data, with a focus on studying the formation of sustainable biohybrid films for energy materials. References: [1] J.E. Heger et al., Nanoscale Horiz. 8, 383-395 (2023) [2] J.E. Heger et al., Adv. Funct. Mater. 32, 2113080 (2022) [3] J.E. Heger et al., JACS Au (2025)

Speaker: Tyler Martin
Title: Discussion on Community Needs
Abstract: This collaborative session focuses on identifying and addressing the evolving needs of the machine learning for X-ray and neutron science community. Participants will discuss challenges in data analysis pipelines, accessibility of ML tools, training needs, and opportunities for cross-facility collaboration. The discussion aims to establish priorities for software development, standardization efforts, and knowledge sharing to accelerate adoption of ML methods across global facilities. Join us to help shape future directions and strengthen connections between researchers, facility scientists, and software developers in our growing community.

Speaker: Austin McDannald
Affiliation: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Title: Autonomous Phase Mapping
Abstract: In this tutorial we’ll show how to build the algorithms for autonomous phase mapping using artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). We’ll show how to frame the problem so that it can be addressed by ML tools. Then walk through a particular example algorithm, showcasing the design decisions and their implications. We’ll show what makes this problem difficult and potential pitfalls. Then we will show alternative ways to frame the problem including automatic phase ID and automatic Rietveld Refinement. Lastly, we’ll discuss future directions of ML and AI techniques for diffraction analysis.

Speaker: Phil Maffetone
Title: Human-in-the-Loop Control of Adaptive and Autonomous Experiments with Bluesky
Abstract: This presentation explores the active work integrating artificial intelligence and robotics at the National Synchrotron Light Source II. Through various case studies, we highlight the optimization of beamline alignment, improved experimental outcomes, and the orchestration of distributed multimodal experiments. This ongoing development includes collaborators from across the light and neutron sources in the DOE complex. We will elaborate on the open-source Bluesky project, and its capabilities to support adaptive and autonomous experiments. Additionally, we will discuss how Bluesky can be integrated with open-source robotic control software to unlock new flexible automation for autonomous scientific research, which scales to new experiments and continues to leverage human ingenuity.

Speaker: Yongqiang (YQ) Cheng
Title: Accelerating vibration and phonon calculations for real-time analysis of inelastic neutron scattering spectra
Abstract: Inelastic neutron scattering (INS) is one of the most powerful techniques for probing vibrational dynamics in materials. A range of instruments and experimental configurations enables measurements of molecular spectroscopy, phonon density of states, and full phonon dispersion. However, a common challenge in INS experiments is the analysis and interpretation of spectral data. Traditional approaches often rely on complex simulations that require substantial computing resources and specialized expertise, making them inefficient and less accessible. Recent advancements in AI/ML for scientific research offer promising alternatives that could transform INS data analysis. In this talk, I will present recent developments and results in this direction. I will introduce a new tool designed for rapid INS simulations and experimental comparisons, demonstrating its capabilities. The real-time capability enabled by AI/ML will have a significant impact on the plan and execution of INS experiments, as well as the post-experiment data analysis.

Speaker: Esther Tsai
Title: Towards AI-accelerated Synchrotron X-ray Experimentation
Abstract: Synchrotron beamlines are constantly in high demand, making efficient beamtime usage and sustainable operations crucial. X-ray scattering beamlines often utilize complex in-situ setups and thus smooth integration and precise control are critical for productive beamtime. Advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning, including the use of large language models, can improve beamline operation efficiency to provide better user support as well as improve human-AI collaboration to accelerate scientific discovery.

Speaker: Wenda Si
Title: Extracting Order Parameters from Neutron Diffraction Data Using Machine Learning
Abstract: Neutron diffraction/diffuse scattering provides an excellent tool to study phase transitions and disorders in materials. Recent advancements in neutron scattering technology have led to a significant increase in the volume of neutron diffraction/diffuse data, surpassing the capacity for human analysis. Unsupervised learning methods, such as Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), are particularly effective for analyzing neutron data, especially in identifying order parameters of weak peaks that may be obscured by background noise. While similar technologies have been successfully applied to X-ray diffraction data processing (X-TEC), methods for neutron data analysis remain limited. Here, we developed a Mantid-based GMM clustering model and apply it to neutron diffraction data on the metal halide double perovskites, Cs2AgBiBr6, to investigate its order parameter and phase transitions at low temperature. The obtained order parameters have the same trend as those measured by triple-axis spectrometer, and a second-order structural phase transition due to phonon softening is identified.

Speaker: Joseph McCourt
Title: CNN-enhanced Nanostructure Characterization via Combined X-ray Ptychography and SAXS Imaging (pty-co-SAXS)
Abstract: Multi-length scale structure characterization is required for hierarchical samples ranging from energy storage and catalysis to biological and bio-inspired systems because morphology as well as local arrangements of nanostructures affect physical properties of materials. X-ray scattering techniques, such as SAXS, have provided powerful tools to study internal structures, but the obtained information is typically the ensemble average over the sample area covered by the x-ray beam, which would limit a full understanding of local diverse arrangements of nanostructures. The unique capability of x-ray ptychography to probe both surface and internal structures of samples at a high-spatial resolution makes it attractive to combine with SAXS which shares a similar measurement geometry. With this combination of pty-co-SAXS, ptychography can provide morphology at nano-scale resolution across micron-to-mm size sample, while SAXS provides reciprocal-space information revealing nanostructure size, shape, and orientation in a length scale smaller than hundreds of nanometers and even down to sub-nanometer. Typically, with a focused beam in a SAXS geometry, the Δq resolution would be compromised for spatial resolution as diffraction peaks will be significantly convolved by a diverging beam due to the used focusing optics (e.g. Fresnel zone plate). However, in pty-co-SAXS, a quantitative beam profile will be recovered at the sample plane, which can be used to deconvolute the SAXS data using a convolutional neural network (CNN). A revolutionary increase in brightness and coherent flux promised by the upgrade of the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Laboratory will greatly contribute to improved imaging capabilities via ptychography which requires high coherent flux and SAXS which benefits from high probe intensity. Altogether, this work presents how by utilizing our proposed combined approach, we can correlate the information collected by the two techniques from a single sample environment ideally with a single detector while minimizing radiation dose.

Speaker: Tyler Martin & Peter Beaucage
Affiliation: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Title: Using AFL software to enable autonomous small angle scattering
Abstract: The Autonomous Formulation Lab (AFL) is a National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) program that seeks to accelerate the discovery and optimization of soft materials through the development and application of autonomous techniques to small angle X-ray and neutron scattering. One path towards widespread adoption of autonomous techniques is through the development of accessible software that lowers the bar to running autonomous experiments. In this interactive tutorial, we will demonstrate how to use AFL software to accomplish two tasks related to building robotic autonomous platforms: (a) using the `AFL.automation.APIServer` to covert a local piece of hardware (e.g., motor, measurement, robotic platform) into a network addressable device with a task queue and (b) using `AFL.double_agent` to build a decision agent that can interpret small angle scattering data and make decisions about the course of an experiment.

Speaker: Maria K. Chan
Title: Data- and theory-informed approaches for accelerating the capture and interpretation of core-level spectra
Abstract: The use of advanced, including in situ and operando, core-level spectroscopy techniques has enabled detailed characterization of materials during synthesis and operations. Data-driven approaches, especially guided by computational spectroscopy, enable robust and accelerated information extraction from such spectroscopy data. In this talk, we discuss the featurization of x-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) for extraction of local structure and electronic properties in battery cathode materials [1], and the extension thereof towards the detection of antisite defect and oxygen vacancy from multimodal EELS/XANES [2]. We also discuss the use of data-driven approaches to accelerate the acquisition [3] and analysis [4] of XANES mapping data. Finally, we discuss the use of AI to extract relevant labeled microscopy and spectroscopy data from scientific literature [5], and recent extensions involving the use of large language models and multi-model contrastive learning. Speaker: Zhongcan Xiao
Title: Background removal methods in neutron scattering data based on machine learning methods
Abstract: In neutron scattering data, background noise significantly impedes the accurate analysis of the material properties. We present two machine learning-based methods for background noise removal. One method is KD-Tree. Estimation of background and Ring Feature Extraction with a non-uniform Gaussian fitting model. The KD-Tree Estimation method utilizes background data collected from measurement without the sample, which is a matrix in 3D reciprocal space. Then we partition data using a KD-Tree structure into different sub-regions based on variance, size, and other features of the data in the sub-region. This way we obtain a data structure with background noise in each region. The background removal to the sample-containing measurement data is then performed with the KD-Tree estimation of background. The second method is Ring Feature Extraction with a non-uniform Gaussian fitting model. It addresses large-scale, slowly varying ring artifacts arising from aluminum sample containers. By extracting radial and angular features from background measurements, we construct a non-uniform Gaussian fitting model to estimate the intensity and variation of the background. This model is then used to subtract the background from experimental data. Both methods have been tested and demonstrated to effectively remove background noise, enhancing data quality and making them well-suited for different neutron scattering applications.

Speaker: Wiebke Koepp
Title: Driving Autonomous Experiments with Machine Learning-Based Workflows
Abstract: Autonomous experiments are guided by objectives, often derived through multiple data reduction steps. These objectives can be analytically defined, for example based on peak positions or intensity measures, or generated through machine learning workflows, such as spatial segmentation or embeddings of raw measurement data into lower-dimensional spaces that capture similarity. In this talk, I will share our experience developing workflow infrastructure to support both types of objectives and their application in experiments conducted at beamlines at the Advanced Light Source and other collaborating facilities.

Speaker: Sean Gasiorowski
Title: Adaptive Targeting of Materials Science Experiments using Bayesian Experimental Design
Abstract: Materials discovery is driven by searches over multi-dimensional processing and synthesis conditions. However, experimental budgets are finite, and individual experiments may take non-trivial setup and processing time. Even simulation studies of materials systems can be expensive, costing hours of computation per simulation, which can result in weeks of computation for large surveys or optimization procedures. Selectively choosing which experiments to perform is crucial in order to meet experimental goals. We present results using sequential Bayesian experimental design to do such selection. We focus in particular on Bayesian Algorithm Execution (BAX), which aims to maximize the expected information gain about computable function objectives, and highlight the utility of BAX relative to standard Bayesian optimization. We emphasize the strengths of an “AI-in-the-loop” methodology, in which guided experimentation can be used to build experimenter intuition about complex relationships between condition variables. We demonstrate our methodology in recent work on materials subset estimation, as well as ongoing work in catalysis optimization and studies of pressure and strain-driven metastable perovskite states.

Speaker: Christopher Tassone
Title: ML Enabled Data Analysis and Experimental Steering for Autonomous Measurements
Abstract: Rapid discovery and synthesis of advanced materials increasingly depend on machine learning methods capable of efficiently navigating vast experimental design spaces. While machine learning predictions hold great potential for identifying materials with targeted properties, practical adoption is hindered by extensive experimental validation requirements, limited availability of synthesis data, and underreported unsuccessful syntheses. To address these challenges, we introduce a closed-loop, machine learning-driven framework that accelerates synthetic discovery despite limited prior data or incomplete synthetic knowledge. Our approach combines intuitive, user-defined filtering algorithms with intelligent, parameter-free, sequential data acquisition strategies (SwitchBAX, InfoBAX, and MeanBAX), eliminating the need for complex, task-specific acquisition functions. Additionally, we present convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) trained on nearly one million crystal structures from the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database and the Cambridge Structural Database, demonstrating accurate, automated estimation of lattice parameters from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) data, significantly reducing the unit-cell search space by factors of 100–1000. Systematic analysis indicates that realistic experimental conditions—particularly impurity phases, baseline noise, and peak broadening—pose notable challenges to model accuracy, yet appropriate data modification techniques effectively mitigate these issues.

Speaker: Lilo Pozzo
Title: Optimization of Colloidal Nanomaterials Synthesis with AI-Driven Experiments and Accessible Automation
Abstract: The synthesis of nanomaterials (e.g. SiO2, ZnO) using sol-gel and nucleation-growth processes is strongly affected by a large number of parameters (e.g. pH, concentrations, temperatures, mixing, surfactants) in a complex and large design space. This can be an advantage, due to the high-tunnability of the desired material structure and properties, and a curse since it can lead to the slow and costly exploration of vast design spaces, and can cause confusion in the interpretation of relationships between synthesis parameters and outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI), when paired with accessible laboratory automation, can greatly accelerate materials optimization and scientific discovery in complex systems such as these. For example, it can efficiently map phase-diagrams with intelligent sampling along phase boundaries, or in ‘retrosynthesis’ problems where a material with a target structure is desired but a synthetic route is not yet known. In this work, we employ an open, accessible and flexible automation platform called ‘Jubilee’ and interface it with advanced characterization tools such as spectroscopy, dynamic light scattering (DLS), and small angle x-ray scattering (SAXS) to help accelerate the efficient exploration of large design spaces. Advanced data science and AI tools are also integrated and used to accelerate the interpretation of results and to propose optimized searching of the unkown design space to maximize the information value of future sampling campaigns. We demonstrate this integrated approach using examples of sol-gel synthesis of ceramic nanomaterials, metal nanoparticles, and new metal chalcogenides. This approach is generalizable and can help accelerate nanomaterials research in every laboratory through the democratization of automation and the adoption of open source practices.

Speaker: Zhuowen Zhao
Title: Seeing Deep into Cells with Cryo-Electron Tomography and AI
Abstract: At the Chan Zuckerberg Imaging Institute, we are developing technologies to advance the imaging of cells using Cryo-Electron Tomography (Cryo-ET), which enables visualization of biomolecular structures in their native cellular environment. A major bottleneck of the current pipeline is the localization of similar structures across hundreds of tomograms—a multi-class classification task, commonly known as particle picking. In this talk, I will first describe our efforts in hosting a global machine learning challenge that drove substantial innovations for particle picking. Then, I will discuss an ongoing work on localization and refinement of putative protein complexes using Boltz-1, a reimplementation of AlphaFold3.

Speaker: Wiebke Koepp & Tanny Chavez
Title: Bridging Experiment and Analysis: Machine Learning Tools for Real-Time Labeling, Exploration, and Cross-Facility Learning
Abstract: As scientific user facilities generate increasingly complex and high-throughput datasets, the need for computational tools that support seamless, scalable data analysis has never been greater. This demo introduces a suite of machine learning (ML) tools developed to enhance experiment workflows through accelerated data labeling, interactive latent space exploration, and high-resolution image segmentation. Our framework allows researchers to explore experimental datasets in real time, supporting informed decision-making during data collection. Complementing this, we showcase segmentation workflows tailored for large, high-resolution scientific images, enabling accurate and efficient analysis as part of the broader experimental pipeline. Deployed at the Advanced Light Source (ALS) and collaborating facilities, these tools help bridge the gap between data collection and interpretation, accelerating the path from experiment to insight.

Speaker: Petrus Zwart
Title: Get Better Data
Abstract: This talk explores how uncertainty quantification (UQ), advanced denoising methods, and autonomous experimentation can work together to get better data—either during an experiment or in post-processing. By combining principled confidence estimation with modern image reconstruction and adaptive sampling strategies, we can improve both the quality and efficiency of scientific measurements. The focus is on practical approaches that make data collection smarter, faster, and more impactful, enabling researchers to make better decisions with fewer, but more meaningful, measurements.

Speaker: Graham Roberts
Title: Machine Learning Accelerated Small Angle Scattering Analysis
Abstract: Small angle scattering (SAS) is a powerful tool for the characterization of nanoparticles. The equipment required to gather these data have improved dramatically although analysis of curves remains time consuming. We present an automatic and efficient workflow for analysis of both the morphology and structure of nanoparticles leveraging simple and efficient machine learning models. Additionally we demonstrate methods by which experimentalists may customize the model to suite any particular experiment. This approach allows an expert to incorporate their knowledge of a system in conjunction with ML models. This workflow allows an expert to efficiently create powerful ML tools to accelerate their SAS experiments.

Speaker: Lina Zhao
Affiliation: Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Title: Bayesian Deep Learning for XRD Phase Identification: Uncertainty Quantification and Physically Interpretable Pattern Analysis in Perovskite Materials
Abstract: X-ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis, while pivotal for characterizing atomic structures and defects in materials, faces critical limitations due to complex pattern interpretation, data scarcity, and the opaque nature of conventional deep learning models. This study introduces a Bayesian deep learning framework to address these challenges, focusing on uncertainty-aware predictions and physically interpretable decision-making. We first construct a synthetic perovskite dataset using Template Element Replacement, spanning 93 space groups and 53 chemical formulas, which enhances classification accuracy by 5% compared to traditional datasets. A Bayesian-enhanced VGGNet (B-VGGNet) is then developed to quantify prediction uncertainty, achieving 84% accuracy in space group classification and 98% accuracy in structure-type identification on experimental data. Entropy analysis reveals 92% of predictions exhibit near-zero uncertainty, demonstrating high confidence. For interpretability, feature importance mapping via clustering identifies critical XRD patterns aligned with the seven major crystal systems, ensuring adherence to crystallographic principles. The framework’s innovations include: 1) A scalable dataset generation method for underrepresented materials, 2) Integrated Bayesian uncertainty quantification to mitigate overconfidence, and 3) Physically grounded interpretability through symmetry-sensitive feature attribution. Validated against experimental and synthetic benchmarks, this approach advances autonomous XRD analysis by balancing algorithmic transparency, reliability, and domain-specific fidelity, enabling broader adoption in materials discovery and quality control.

Speaker: Alessandro Sepe FRSC
Affiliation: Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF), Shanghai Advanced Research Institute (SARI), Chinese Academy of Sciences
Title: Scientific IaaS in the era of Big Data, AI and Robotic Automation
Abstract: A synchrotron has the advantage of being able to reveal the complex interconnections between matter structure and matter properties in real-time. It produces the kind of Big Data that scientists need to address fundamental questions in all fields of the nanotechnologies. In this context national Synchrotron facilities such as the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF) in China play a crucial role for a wide range of multidisciplinary scientific communities and industries. The rapid development of synchrotron, neutron, laser and X-ray Free Electron Laser (XFEL) facilities, among others, has massively increased the speed with which experiments can be performed, and increased the amount of raw data collected during each experiment. While this has created enormous new opportunities, it has also created tremendous challenges for the national facilities and the users. As a consequence, only a small fraction of this multidisciplinary and scientifically complex Big Data are fully analyzed and, ultimately, used in scientific publications and technological applications. This effect, commonly known as the “data deluge”, affects the light sources in several different ways. Nowadays, we are witnessing the dawn of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML) and Robotic Automation within the field of large scientific facilities, generating profound changes in how petabytes of interdisciplinary datasets are intelligently processed, managed, analyzed and visualized. Therefore, the evolution of large scientific facilities into Superfacilities enables multidisciplinary user science confronting the Big Data challenges, fundamental for the entire scientific community. To address these crucial Big Data challenges that affect large scientific facilities world-wide, the Big Data Science Center (BDSC) at SSRF has architected, developed and successfully deployed a cutting-edge scientific computing infrastructure, hybridizing large facility science with high-performance computing (HPC) technologies, aiming to provide a scientific Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), and effectively creating the first Superfacility in China, and one of the first worldwide.

Speaker: Lingzhu Bian
Affiliation: Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Title: Unsupervised clustering for extracting fine structural information in ARPES
Abstract: With the rapid development of synchrotron radiation sources, the new generation of light sources can focus the light spot to the micron and even nanometer level, realizing the combination of "microscopy" and "spectroscopy", and providing strong support for high spatial resolution scanning spectroscopy experiments. Spatially resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) is a typical scanning spectroscopy experiment. Spatially resolved ARPES (μ-ARPES,n-ARPES) allows measurements on relatively inhomogeneous surfaces, due to its sub-micrometer beam size. However, challenges remain due to the complexity of the surface, particularly in positioning the area of interest，which only relies on the scanning photoemission microscopy (SPEM). However, the SPEM data is quite heavy, which needs to be well analyzed in order to distinguish the desired regions. This is important but time consuming. Unsupervised clustering method has shown strong capabilities in automatically categorizing the ARPES spatial mapping dataset. However, there is still room for improvement in distinguishing subtle differences caused by different layers and substrates. Here, we propose a method called Multi-Stage Clustering Algorithm (MSCA). Using the K-means clustering results/metrics for real space in different energy-momentum windows as the input of the second round K-means clustering for momentum space, the energy-momentum windows that exhibit subtle inhomogeneity in real space will be highlighted. It recognizes different types of electronic structures both in real space and momentum space in spatially resolved ARPES dataset. This method can be used to capture the areas of interest, and is especially suitable for samples with complex band dispersions, and can be a practical tool to any high dimensional scientific data analysis.

Speaker: Chun Li
Affiliation: Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Title: A machine learning-assisted automatic loop centering software for macromolecular crystallography beamlines
Abstract: Synchrotron light source facilities worldwide are evolving into the fourth generation, equipped with diffraction-limited storage rings. These machines generate high quality X-rays with intense brightness, low emittance, ultrafast pulse, and highly coherent beams, offering extreme spatial and temporal resolving power that enables multiscale and ultra-fast characterizations. Consequently, the experimental mode at next-generation beamlines is shifting from static to high-throughput, multimodal, cross-dimensional and dynamic characterizations, greatly facilitating significant scientific outputs. However, regardless of instrumentation advancements, the development of software and algorithms is still lagging behind, becoming the limiting factor to fully unleash the capabilities these facilities have to offer. Cutting-edge light source facilities desire cutting-edge software and algorithms to complement, particularly in key areas such as autonomous beam adjustment and experiment control, intelligent experimental steering and scanning path prediction, data acquisition and orchestration, data analysis and interpretation. Today, we are entering the “fourth paradigm” driven by big data, where artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning plays a crucial role in advancing scientific discovery (AI for Science). Integrating advanced machine learning techniques into a universal large-scale scientific software system designed for next-generation synchrotron facilities, can ultimately solve the limitations on the software end. This talk first briefly presents our latest effort to develop such large-scale software system (Mamba) designed for China’s first fourth-generation light source; then the talk will introduce our recent work on machine learning-empowered automatic loop centering process using SwinTransformer with YOLO object detection models, which is designed for macromolecular crystallography (MX) beamlines. This subject is influential to reduce the man power and labor manually conducted at MX beamlines if one needs to align the X-ray beam with the sample, especially when there exist multiple samples on a single sample plate. The centering process is divided into two stages: automatic loop detection and intelligent crystal recognition. We are integrating the centering process into the software system Mamba with a graphical user interface (GUI) to streamline the centering process at MX beamlines, forming a dedicated software tool to beamline users with detailed operation tutorials provided. Our most recent developmental progress on the centering procedures and the software tool will both be reported. We hope this talk will facilitate inter-institutional cooperation on the development of machine learning-empowered autonomous experiment control system, particularly on those systems relying on automatic and intelligent machine learning object detection and recognition techniques at photon and neutron (PaN) large scale facilities.

Speaker: Fei Zhan
Affiliation: Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Science
Title: A Graph neural network-based approach to 3D structure analysis of X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy
Abstract: X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) is an indispensable tool to characterize the atomic-scale local 3D structure of the system. Here, we present an approach to simulate XANES based on a customized 3D graph neural network (3DGNN) model, XAS3Dabs, which takes directly the 3D structure of the system as input, and the inherent relation between the fine structure of spectrum and local geometry is considered during the model construction. It turns out to be faster than the traditional XANES fitting method when the simulation approach and XANES optimization algorithm are combined to fit the 3D structure of the given system. XAS3Dabs model can be generalized to simulate the spectra for the systems with the absorber having the designed absorption edge so as to meet the expectations of online data processing.

Speaker: Masashi Ishii
Affiliation: National Institute for Materials Science, NIMS
Title: MDR XAFS DB: X-ray absorption data integration for meta-spectral analysis
Abstract: MDR XAFS DB is a data integration infrastructure created to share XAFS spectra widely, with data provided by six organizations in Japan. In order to operate the data in accordance with the FAIR principles, the following efforts have been made: (1) Machine-readable structured metadata is attached to all spectra. (2) Cross-sectional searches are made possible by normalizing the material vocabulary using a dictionary. (3) In order to permanently retain and discover data, DOIs are attached to all spectra. (4) Machine-accessible APIs are developed and batch downloads are made possible. In this presentation, we introduce the details of the MDR XAFS DB and frontier research on materials informatics using it, and describe the current state of data-driven infrastructure and the scope for global data collaboration.

Speaker: Frank Schreiber
Title: Machine learning for surface scattering: Concepts, challenges, and solutions
Abstract: Surface scattering is an indispensable tool [1]. Modern sources enable even time-resolved experiments, producing large data sets in short time [2]. Machine learning (ML) techniques offer a data filtering and analysis strategy complementary to conventional approaches [3-10]. We first provide a brief summary of different surface scattering geometries (reflectometry (NR/XRR); grazing-incidence wide / small angle scattering (GISANS/GISAXS/GIWAXS)). Second, we discuss our ML solution for NR/XRR and explain why this seemingly simple, essentially one-dimensional problem is actually more difficult, and why some other approaches have failed. We present our most recent solutions for NR/XRR [6,10], including the “normalizing flows” strategy for the incorporation of distributions of parameters for the solution, which allows to quantify error bars. Third, we present our ML strategy for grazing-incidence scattering data, including the specifics of the geometry with distortions of the data, which can be challenging for ML-based feature recognition. Fourth, we outline our efforts for ML data analysis pipelines employable at public instruments, including closed-loop experimental control with feedback of the ML-based analysis for the experiment [11]. Last, we point out the role of big-data projects such as DAPHNE4NFDI, data base projects such as https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6497437 (Reflectometry Curves (XRR and NR) and Corresponding Fits for Machine Learning) and other joint efforts of the community. Speaker: Thorsten Hellert
Title: Developing specialized text embedding models for (accelerator-)physics
Abstract: The specialized terminology and complex concepts inherent in physics present significant challenges for Natural Language Processing (NLP), particularly when relying on general-purpose models. In this talk, I will discuss the development of physics-specific text embedding models designed to overcome these obstacles, beginning with PhysBERT—the first model pre-trained exclusively on a curated corpus of 1.2 million arXiv physics papers. Building upon this foundation, we turn our attention to accelerator physics, a subfield with even more intricate language and concepts. To effectively capture the nuances of this domain, we developed AccPhysBERT, a sentence embedding model fine-tuned specifically for accelerator physics literature. A key aspect of this development involved leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) extensively to generate annotated training data, enabling AccPhysBERT to facilitate advanced NLP applications such as semantic paper-reviewer matching and integration into Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems.

Speaker: Stefan Kowarik
Title: Neural Networks in Surface Crystallography: A New Paradigm for GIWAXS Analysis
Abstract: We present a neural network (NN)-based approach for Grazing Incidence Wide-Angle X-ray Scattering (GIWAXS) analysis that significantly accelerates surface crystallography while minimizing the need for human input. By training the NN on crystallographic databases and refining predictions using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques, the method achieves far below sub-angstrom and sub-degree accuracy in predicting unit cell parameters of crystalline thin films in most examples. In contrast to conventional methods, our approach eliminates the need for measuring the missing wedge via specular scans—GIWAXS data alone is sufficient. Beyond unit cell determination, the NN enables rapid and robust identification of the contact plane’s Miller indices, even for complex real-world materials. We demonstrate the method’s effectiveness on real data from perovskites, metal-organic frameworks, and molecular thin films.

Speaker: Gohar Ali Siddiqui
Title: Incorporating experimental data for ML-assisted dynamics simulations.
Abstract: I will discuss how machine learning techniques can be used to bias dynamics simulations and accelerate sampling. The will in future enable us to incorporate experimental data , which often can be noisy or incomplete. Integrating it with simulation results can be a complex task. However, by leveraging machine learning algorithms, it becomes possible to identify hidden patterns, fill in missing information, and reconcile experimental measurements with theoretical models. This integration can enable the creation of a unified data stream that provides a comprehensive view of material performance, encompassing both simulated predictions and real-world observations.

Speaker: Yufeng Zhai
Title: Deep Learning-Driven GISAXS Data Processing for Nanostructure Characterization
Abstract: Nanostructured materials, are at the forefront of advanced applications in various fields, owing to their unique physical and chemical properties. Grazing incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) has emerged as a powerful technique for probing the morphology of these nanostructures, offering valuable insights into electron density distributions both at the surface and within thin films. In our approach, we first simulate GISAXS pattern using the Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA) model to generate high-quality training datasets. We then apply deep learning techniques, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), to predict size distributions from GISAXS data. Our results demonstrate that CNNs are highly robust under varying noise conditions and present a promising, time-efficient approach for overcoming the challenges of conventional scattering analysis. This study highlights the potential of integrating advanced computational methods and new analytical tools to enhance the characterization of nanostructures.

Title: Workshop Report on Autonomous Methodologies for Accelerating X-ray Measurements
Abstract: The National Institute of Standards and Technology and the International Centre for Diffraction Data co-hosted a workshop on 17-18 October 2023 to identify and prioritize the goals, challenges, and opportunities for critical and emerging technology needs within industry, with an emphasis on leveraging artificial intelligence, data-driven methodologies, and high-throughput and automated workflows for accelerating x-ray-based structural analysis for materials development and manufacturing. Participants, predominantly from industry, gathered in-person at ICDD headquarters in Newtown Square, Pennsylvania. This talk presents the findings of this workshop report, which provide critical input for strategic planning and the convening activities, and serve as a kickoff for future public-private cooperation.

Speaker: Peter Müller-Buschbaum
Title: Discussion on Community Needs
Abstract: This collaborative session focuses on identifying and addressing the evolving needs of the machine learning for X-ray and neutron science community. Participants will discuss challenges in data analysis pipelines, accessibility of ML tools, training needs, and opportunities for cross-facility collaboration. The discussion aims to establish priorities for software development, standardization efforts, and knowledge sharing to accelerate adoption of ML methods across global facilities. Join us to help shape future directions and strengthen connections between researchers, facility scientists, and software developers in our growing community.
